title: Types of variables and the conceptual model
summary: Dependent, independent, extraneous, control, moderator and mediator variables, the conceptual framework that links them, and the four-day working week examples.

chunks.heading: Independent and dependent variables
chunks.explanation_md:
Start with the main pair.

- If one variable **depends upon or is a consequence of** another variable, it is the **dependent variable**.
- The variable that is **antecedent to** (comes before) the dependent variable is the **independent variable**.

So the independent variable is the one you think of as the starting point, and the dependent variable is the result you are studying.

The research terms slide also lists the full set of **types of variables**: **Independent, Dependent, Extraneous, Control, Moderating, Compounding and Intervening**. This topic covers the ones the deck defines on its own slide.

chunks.heading: Extraneous and control variables
chunks.explanation_md:
- **Extraneous variables** are **independent variables that are not considered for the study's purpose but may affect the dependent variable**.
- **Control variables** are **used to minimise the effects of extraneous variables**. They are **measured, but their effect is not hypothesised**.

The slide adds a simple way to see control variables: they are variables **you are not particularly interested in**, but they **can have a material effect on your dependent variable**, and you **wish to eliminate their effects** from the effect of your independent variable of interest on your dependent variable.

chunks.heading: Moderator vs mediator
chunks.explanation_md:
Read these two carefully.

**Moderator variables** are like control variables, but **instead of having an effect on other variables, they impact the relationship between variables**. They are **measured, and their effect is hypothesised**.

The slide's simple picture: **consider moderating variables as catalysts that make a relationship between independent and dependent variables stronger or weaker**.

**Mediator variables**: **a mediating variable (or mediator) explains how two variables are related**.

**Control vs moderator:** both are measured, but a control variable's effect is **not hypothesised**, while a moderator's effect **is hypothesised**.

chunks.heading: The conceptual model: how the variables fit together
chunks.explanation_md:
The **Conceptual Model** slide shows a **conceptual framework example** that puts the variables on one map:

- An arrow runs from the **independent variable** to the **dependent variable**.
- The **moderating variable** sits above and points onto **that arrow**: it acts on the relationship.
- The **mediating variable** sits in between: the independent variable points to it, and it points on to the dependent variable.
- The **control variable** points straight to the **dependent variable**.
chunks.exam_line: Conceptual framework: independent to dependent variable; moderator acts on that arrow; mediator sits between them; control variable points to the dependent variable.

chunks.heading: Four-day working week: moderator and mediator examples
chunks.explanation_md:
The deck uses one study idea to show both.

**Moderating variable example:** *The introduction of a four-day working week (IV) will lead to higher productivity (DV), especially among younger workers (MV).*
- **IV**: four-day working week.
- **DV**: productivity.
- **MV**: **workers' age**. It points onto the IV to DV arrow: the effect shows especially among younger workers.

**Mediating variable example:** *The introduction of a four-day working week (IV) will lead to higher productivity (DV) by increasing job satisfaction (IVV) (Mediating variable).*
- The chain is **four-day working week** to **job satisfaction** to **productivity**. Job satisfaction explains **how** the four-day week leads to higher productivity.
- The fuller diagram also shows **MV: workers' age** on the job satisfaction to productivity arrow, **CV: weather** pointing to productivity (dashed), **IVV: routine work** pointing onto the job satisfaction to productivity arrow (dashed), and **CFV: meeting attendance** pointing to routine work (dashed).
chunks.exam_line: Moderator: four-day week (IV) raises productivity (DV) especially among younger workers (MV: workers' age). Mediator: four-day week raises productivity by increasing job satisfaction (IVV).

questions.stem: Differentiate between a moderator variable and a mediator variable, using the four-day working week example.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both variables sit around the link between an independent and a dependent variable, but they do different jobs.

- **Moderator variable:** does not affect other variables directly; it **impacts the relationship** between them, acting like a **catalyst** that makes the relationship **stronger or weaker**. It is measured and its effect is hypothesised.
- **Mediator variable:** **explains how** two variables are related; the effect passes through it.
- **Moderator example:** a four-day working week (IV) leads to higher productivity (DV), **especially among younger workers**. Workers' age is the MV.
- **Mediator example:** a four-day working week (IV) leads to higher productivity (DV) **by increasing job satisfaction**. Job satisfaction is the mediator.

So a moderator changes how strong the link is, while a mediator is the path the link travels through.

rubric.point: Moderator impacts the relationship, makes it stronger or weaker
Mediator explains how two variables are related
Moderator example: workers' age
Mediator example: job satisfaction

questions.stem: Distinguish between extraneous variables and control variables.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both deal with influences outside the main relationship being studied.

- **Extraneous variables:** independent variables that are **not considered for the study's purpose** but **may affect the dependent variable**.
- **Control variables:** used to **minimise the effects of extraneous variables**. They are **measured, but their effect is not hypothesised**.
- **Purpose:** a researcher is not particularly interested in control variables, but they can have a material effect on the dependent variable, so their effect is removed from the effect of the independent variable of interest.

In short, extraneous variables are the problem and control variables are the way of handling it.

questions.stem: Explain the types of variables used in research and show how they fit together in a conceptual model.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **variable** is a symbol of an event, act, characteristic, trait or attribute that can be measured or assigned categorical values. The slides describe several types.

**Types of variables:**
- **Dependent variable:** depends upon or is a consequence of another variable.
- **Independent variable:** antecedent to the dependent variable.
- **Extraneous variables:** independent variables not considered for the study's purpose that may still affect the dependent variable.
- **Control variables:** used to minimise the effects of extraneous variables; **measured, but their effect is not hypothesised**.
- **Moderator variables:** **impact the relationship** between variables, like a catalyst making it stronger or weaker; **measured, and their effect is hypothesised**.
- **Mediator variables:** **explain how** two variables are related.

**The conceptual model:**
- An arrow runs from the **independent variable** to the **dependent variable**.
- The **moderating variable** points down onto the **middle of that arrow**, because it changes the relationship itself.
- The independent variable also points to the **mediating variable**, which points on to the dependent variable, because the effect passes through it.
- The **control variable** points directly to the **dependent variable**, because its effect on the outcome is what the researcher wants to remove.

**Conclusion:** the conceptual model is a map of the study, showing which variable causes which, what changes the strength of the link, what carries the effect, and what must be held constant.

questions.stem: A firm believes that introducing a four-day working week will raise productivity. Using the professor's diagrams, identify the independent, dependent, moderating, mediating and control variables, and explain the role of each.
questions.model_answer_md:
The slides use the four-day working week to show every type of variable in one study.

- **Independent variable (IV): four-day working week.** It is the antecedent the firm introduces.
- **Dependent variable (DV): productivity.** It is the consequence the firm wants to change.
- **Moderating variable (MV): workers' age.** The claim is that productivity rises **especially among younger workers**, so age makes the IV to DV link **stronger or weaker**. It is measured and its effect is hypothesised.
- **Mediating variable (IVV): job satisfaction.** The week raises productivity **by increasing job satisfaction**, so it explains **how** the IV affects the DV.
- **Control variable (CV): weather.** It may affect productivity, but the firm is not interested in it, so it is measured to **remove its effect** without being hypothesised.

**Other links in the diagram:** routine work points onto the job satisfaction to productivity arrow, and meeting attendance (CFV) points to routine work.

**Conclusion:** separating the variables lets the firm test whether the four-day week works, for whom it works best and through what route, while keeping outside effects such as weather out of the result.
